<!-- What the curator's public work as `palimondo` (Stack Overflow, the Swift benchmark suite, the Swift forums, GitHub) shows he knew and when, gathered on 2026-10-16 from 32 web requests, so that the coordinator can calibrate its explanations to him. -->

# The curator's public work, as `palimondo`

Gathered on 2026-10-16 by a Sonnet worker, at the curator's word. Nothing was logged into or posted, and no address of his was used.

How reliable each source is:

- **Stack Overflow and the Swift forums** were read as the sites' own JSON (the Stack Exchange API; the forum's search JSON), so their counts and dates are exact. WebFetch refused `api.stackexchange.com`, so the API and the forum JSON were fetched with `curl` through the platform's proxy; those requests are inside the 32.
- **GitHub pages** came through WebFetch's summarizer, which restates the page and can slip (its own count of unmerged pull requests on page 1 was 4 where its rows show 5). Titles and numbers below are as the listings show them; I did not check them against the git history. A date beside a pull request is the date its listing shows, which is the merge date, or the close date for one closed unmerged, not the date it was opened.
- GitHub's API was closed to this session (the proxy allows only the session's own repositories), and the forum refused the profile summary page (`/u/palimondo/summary.json`, 403, twice; cause not known). So the forum's total post count is unknown; the list below is what the search returned.

## 1. Stack Overflow, user 41307

Profile: https://stackoverflow.com/users/41307/palimondo. Account since 2008-11-27, last seen 2026-04-21, reputation 7,411 (4 gold, 44 silver, 59 bronze badges), accept rate 83 %.

**Volume and years.** 45 answers, the first on 2009-06-03 and the last on 2023-07-27; by year: 2009 3, 2010 2, 2011 11, 2012 12, 2013 6, 2014 5, then 6 in all from 2015 to 2023 (2015 1, 2017 1, 2018 1, 2019 2, 2023 1). So 34 of the 45 are from 2011 to 2014. 24 questions, from 2009-06-29 to 2018-05-15 (the last of them in 2018; 2011 4, 2012 5, 2014 4 are the busy years).

**Topics** (the API's top tags; an answer counts in each of its tags):

- iOS and Objective-C carry most of it: `ios` 15 answers and 6 questions, `objective-c` 13 answers, `iphone` 10, `autolayout` 5, `core-animation` 3 questions (score 79 together), `core-graphics`, `cashapelayer`, `nsstring`.
- Swift: 5 answers (score 82 together). The first Swift answer in the top five is from 2014-06-12, ten days after Swift was announced (2014-06-02, from my own knowledge, not from the API).
- Scala: 3 questions (score 121 together) and 1 answer, all from 2009 and 2010, including the Lift framework; two of the three questions ask what a feature costs.
- Java: one question, 2009.

**The five highest-voted answers** (score; the question answered; date):

| Score | Question | Date | Answer |
|---|---|---|---|
| 78 | What is the meaning of colon, underscore and star in lift's SiteMap(entries:_*)? (Scala, Lift; his own question, answered by him about 25 minutes after he asked it) | 2009-07-14 | https://stackoverflow.com/a/1124172 |
| 66 | Applying a Gradient to CAShapeLayer (Core Graphics) | 2011-08-31 | https://stackoverflow.com/a/7264787 |
| 47 | Shortcuts in Objective-C to concatenate NSStrings | 2012-03-16 | https://stackoverflow.com/a/9730316 |
| 39 | Why create "Implicitly Unwrapped Optionals", since that implies you know there's a value? (Swift) | 2014-06-12 | https://stackoverflow.com/a/24186511 |
| 37 | Auto layout invalid after presenting view controller (and many situation) (iOS 7) | 2013-09-06 | https://stackoverflow.com/a/18655965 |

**The five highest-voted questions** he asked (score; date):

| Score | Question | Date | Link |
|---|---|---|---|
| 67 | Restoring animation where it left off when app resumes from background (iOS, Core Animation) | 2011-09-27 | https://stackoverflow.com/q/7568567 |
| 60 | What is the meaning of colon, underscore and star in lift's SiteMap(entries:_*)? | 2009-07-14 | https://stackoverflow.com/q/1124099 |
| 56 | The cost of nested methods (Scala) | 2010-03-20 | https://stackoverflow.com/q/2482326 |
| 34 | Why is non-breaking space not a whitespace character in Java? (Unicode) | 2009-06-29 | https://stackoverflow.com/q/1060570 |
| 11 | Internal implementation of UIView's block-based animation methods | 2014-03-21 | https://stackoverflow.com/q/22556122 |

**What it shows.** In 2009 and 2010 he met Scala as a learner: the star-underscore sequence argument, what a nested method costs (2010-03-20) and what repeated parameters cost ("Cost of using repeated parameters", https://stackoverflow.com/q/2451845, 2010-03-16, score 5) are questions of someone reading Scala and wondering how it runs, not of someone writing a compiler for it (I read titles and scores only, not the bodies). From 2011 to 2014 he answered iOS framework questions in some depth (animation, gradients, layout), and he asked how UIKit's block animations are built inside. His interest in how a thing is implemented, and in what it costs, is there from 2010. The site is a record of 2009 to 2014; his activity there almost stops after 2014 and moves to the Swift project (below).

## 2. The Swift benchmark suite (`swiftlang/swift`, `benchmark/`)

Search used: https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pulls?q=is%3Apr+author%3Apalimondo (five pages) and the commit lists of two files filtered by his name. He has 102 pull requests in the repository, none open: by the listings' own labels (counted by hand) about 88 merged and 14 closed unmerged. Nearly all carry the tag `[benchmark]`. The merged ones run from 2017-03-30 (https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/8430) to 2020-04-15 (https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/24677, "Janitor Duty: Final Sweep"); the heavy time is 2018-07 to 2019-07. His last commits to the two files below are both from 2019-07-23. Several unmerged ones were closed on 2020-10-05 (https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/26462, https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/30158, https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/30149); the listings give no reason.

**2017: the first pull requests, Python tooling for the suite.**

- The two oldest are small stdlib and benchmark fixes (https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/8429, https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/8430, 2017-04-04 and 2017-03-30).
- `compare_perf_tests.py` and `Benchmark_Driver`: report added and removed benchmarks in a comparison (SR-4601, https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/8991, 2017-04-26); run a subset by prefix (https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/8975, 2017-04-25), by several regular expressions (https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/9026, 2017-05-05), and by ordinal number (https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/10204, 2017-06-14); tie a log to the tested tree's version (SR-4659, https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/8978, 2017-04-27).
- Build side: GYB (the Swift tree's own template tool) in benchmarks (https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/8641, 2017-04-14); drop the jinja2 dependency from the harness generation (SR-4572, https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/9193, 2017-05-11); lint fixes (https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/9998, 2017-05-31).
- Performance of the library itself: `Sequence` internals as a struct instead of a class (https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/9811, 2017-05-24).

**2018: BenchmarkDriver and BenchmarkDoctor, in Python.**

- https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/18719 (opened 2018-08-15, approved 2018-08-20, merged 2018-08-22) adds the classes `BenchmarkDriver`, `BenchmarkDoctor`, `LogParser` and `PerformanceTestSamples` to `benchmark/scripts/Benchmark_Driver` and `compare_perf_tests.py`, with unit tests and a small home-made `Stub`/`Mock` for Python 2.7 (`test_utils.py`). The Doctor checks a benchmark against rules: a naming convention (a 40-character limit, which the maintainer questioned), a runtime under 2,500 microseconds for one iteration, setup overhead above 5 % of the time, and a start on a memory check. `PerformanceTestSamples` can drop outliers by the interquartile-range rule (the commit "Exclude outliers from sample" is from 2018-08-17).
- https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/18924 ("BenchmarkDriver Strangler replaces Benchmark_Driver run", 2018-08-24) replaces the old script piece by piece, the strangler pattern of refactoring. The precursor measured memory with `rusage` instead of parsing `time` output (https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/18124, 2018-07-23).
- Naming and clean-up across the whole suite: a naming convention (https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/20334, 2018-12-13), "Legacy Factor" (https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/20212, 2018-11-06), extract setup from the benchmarks (https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/20048, 2018-11-05), reduce unreasonable setup times (https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/20123, 2018-10-30), and about a dozen "Janitor Duty" pull requests (2018-12 to 2020-04) that make each benchmark run in the target time.
- Lit tests: he fixed and re-enabled the lit tests of the driver (https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/21150, https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/21166, 2018-12-10) and a flaky one (https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/21459, https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/21507, 2018-12-21 and 2019-01-02).

**2018 to 2019: the Swift side, `benchmark/utils/DriverUtils.swift`** (the program that runs and times the benchmarks).

- https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/19097 (merged 2018-09-14; a CI failure in a `LOGFORMAT` test had another committer revert it the same day, https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/19322, and it landed again as https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/19328): a `--quantile` option that prints quantiles of the samples, a `--delta` encoding of them, and some 30 refactoring commits on the same day (`Int` for counts, microseconds, `TestRunner`, the sampling loop, `numIters`, moving the statistics into `BenchResults`). The description gives his reason: the mean and standard deviation assume a normal distribution, which the samples do not have, and the maximum is an outlier that follows the machine's load. A fix of the quantile estimation type followed (https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/19637, 2018-10-01; commit a9f0ce4, 2018-09-20).
- Later commits to the same file: auto-determine the number of samples (67b489d, 2018-10-11), measure the setup function (9d9200e, 2018-10-02), the legacy factor (a7f832f, 2018-11-01), lower the sample cap (9d6f7ad, 2018-12-07), and in July 2019 a minimum sample count, substring filters and measurement metadata in the log (ad24ca4, ec32140, 5571b83). The matching parser commits in `compare_perf_tests.py` are on the same days (the last, cc0e16c, 2019-07-23).

**2019: sampling and statistics.**

- https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/22546 (merged 2019-02-12, fixes SR-9907): raises the minimum number of independent samples before a possible change is reported from 5 to 10, because run-time distributions of some benchmarks have several modes and the minimum is a weak typical value for them. The page names `DataAppendLargeToLarge` as the benchmark that stopped giving false changes.
- https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/26462 ("Robust Measurements", opened 2019-08-02, taken up again 2020-03-02 to 2020-03-04, closed unmerged): the driver samples each benchmark over a fixed time window and keeps up to 102 values (percentiles, minimum, maximum); the run-smoke script gathers independent runs for suspected changes; a commit that picked the most stable of MIN, P05, P10, Q1 and the median by the variance across runs made things worse, which he said in the thread. Reviewers asked whether the noise was the optimizer's instability or the measurement's. Its follow-on "Groundwork" (https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/30158) was closed the same day. This is the one body of work I found that reaches a conclusion about measurement itself, and it ends without landing.
- Reporting: better table headers and right-aligned columns in `ReportFormatter` (https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/25027, 2019-05-24), "Driver Improvements" (https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/26303, 2019-07-24).

**Library performance work beside the benchmarks.**

- https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/25286 (merged 2019-06-11): Lemire's nearly divisionless bounded random integer in the standard library. He reported about four times faster generation on a worst-case bound locally, and CI figures on a 2013 Mac Pro (`RandomShuffleLCG2` 3.23 times faster at `-O`), and noted regressions at `-Onone`; he tried O'Neill's modulo trick and removed it because the generated code did not match the C version. He worked with the reviewer on a 32-bit fallback. He added the SplitMix64 generator to the benchmarks (https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/24357, 2019-04-29).
- ContiguousArray inside `Sequence`'s `dropLast`, `prefix` and `suffix` (https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/21658, 2019-01-08); unit tests for `Set` (https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/pull/24575, 2019-05-09).

**What it shows.** Hands-on, over about three years: Python scripting with unit tests, Swift at the standard-library level, the LLVM style of lit tests, and the practice of measuring a compiler's benchmarks (quantiles, outlier fences, setup overhead, runtime targets, how many independent samples make a change believable, and noise that comes from the machine). None of the pull requests I saw touches the compiler's C++ or its optimizer; he worked on the benchmarks around them and on the library. The work stops in 2019 to 2020.

## 3. The Swift forums (`forums.swift.org`)

His posts: https://forums.swift.org/u/palimondo (the profile page's summary was refused; see the top). The forum's search JSON for `@palimondo` listed 91 topics he posted in, one post shown for each, so the date is of that post: 2017-03-25 to 2019-06-17 (2017 17, 2018 62, 2019 11), then one on 2023-04-30. The topic address is `https://forums.swift.org/t/<id>`. The category names are my reading of the titles. In the lists a date is the day the topic was started, except for the proposal reviews and where I write "his post", where it is the day of his post.

- **Benchmarks and measurement** (the largest group, about 25 topics):
  - "Measuring MEAN Performance (was: Questions about Swift-CI)", https://forums.swift.org/t/6106, 2017-06-12 and 2017-06-13 (page summary): he called comparing minimums fragile for very short tests, proposed the mean with the standard deviation, the coefficient of variation, discarding anomalous samples, and adaptive sampling in `DriverUtils.swift`. Later he built much of this (section 2).
  - "Towards Robust Performance Measurement", https://forums.swift.org/t/11490, started 2018-03-29, his posts to 2019-05-21 (page summary): an outlier fence at the third quartile plus 1.5 times the interquartile range, a five-number summary, a Mann-Whitney U-test for comparing runs (proposed; I did not see it land), a base runtime under 2,500 microseconds, the Doctor's 5 % setup-overhead rule worked out on 2018-04-08 to 2018-04-11, `rusage` for memory (2018-07-12), a claim that no benchmark is noisy in itself and the noise is the environment (2018-08-22), and the maintainer's answer that code alignment, not randomness, made some results unstable (2018-08-24).
  - Also: "Towards Robust Swift Performance", https://forums.swift.org/t/18664 (2018-12-08); "RFC: BenchmarkInfo refactoring", https://forums.swift.org/t/20677 (2019-02-19); "How to profile Swift benchmarks in Instruments", https://forums.swift.org/t/24267 (2019-05-07); "Weird de-optimization in MapReduceClass benchmark", https://forums.swift.org/t/17135 (2018-10-18); "Mysterious memory improvement and regression", https://forums.swift.org/t/5746 (2017-04-21); and, last, "How to view the results of `@swift-ci benchmark`", https://forums.swift.org/t/56563 (topic of 2022-04-06, his post 2023-04-30).
- **Standard-library performance:** "Generating Double values in unit range using Random API is about 45 times slower than necessary", https://forums.swift.org/t/12992 (2018-05-26); "Swift's unpredictable efficiency", https://forums.swift.org/t/13506 (63 posts, from 2018-06-10, his post shown 2018-07-02); "Performance advantage of ContiguousArray", https://forums.swift.org/t/18142 (2018-11-20); "More Representative String Benchmarks", https://forums.swift.org/t/18793 (2018-12-14); "Swift 5's performance with large strings is much slower than 4.2", https://forums.swift.org/t/20603 (2019-02-18); "Performance issues with Foundation.Data", https://forums.swift.org/t/16016 (topic 2018-09-10, his post 2018-10-22).
- **Language and library design** (about 45 topics in the evolution categories: pitches, discussion and proposal reviews), mostly in 2018:
  - Reviews of proposals, among them SE-0193 cross-module inlining and specialization (2018-03-14), SE-0202 random unification (2018-04-04) and two amendment threads on the generator's name (his posts 2018-04-30 and 2018-06-17), SE-0207, SE-0211, SE-0217 "Unwrap or Die" (2018-07-11, a 220-post thread), SE-0223 uninitialized buffer of an array (2018-08-21), SE-0234 removing `Sequence.SubSequence` (2018-11-14), SE-0242 default values for the memberwise initializer (2019-02-22).
  - Pitches and rants about the collection protocols: "[Pitch] Make Collection Super-Convenient and Retire Sequence", https://forums.swift.org/t/12103 (2018-04-24); "Troubling `Sequence`", https://forums.swift.org/t/13130 (2018-06-02); "On the elementsEqual problem, or [Pitch] Set and Dictionary should not be Sequences", https://forums.swift.org/t/12227 (2018-04-28); "RFP: OrderedSet", https://forums.swift.org/t/11399 (2018-03-26); "Add Various Zip-Related Types and Operations", https://forums.swift.org/t/13806 (2018-06-18); "In-place map for MutableCollection", https://forums.swift.org/t/11111 (2018-03-18).
  - On the language itself: "Cascading `mutating` for protocols restricted to reference types", https://forums.swift.org/t/13501 (2018-06-10); "Evolving ABI Stable Language", https://forums.swift.org/t/11968 (2018-04-18); "String's ABI and UTF-8", https://forums.swift.org/t/17676 (2018-11-05); "Single-element labeled tuples?", https://forums.swift.org/t/9797 (2018-02-11).

**What it shows.** An active contributor to the language's public discussion from March 2017 to mid-2019, first about the benchmarks and the CI, from 2018 on about the design of `Sequence`, `Collection`, strings and the random number API. He took part in technical exchanges with the benchmark suite's maintainer (the code-alignment explanation above) and in the review threads of proposals. The forum activity is the same period as the pull requests and ends at about the same time.

## 4. His GitHub repositories (https://github.com/palimondo)

The profile lists 20 public repositories, 6 of his own and 14 forks (the page's own labels; for a fork the date is its last update, not the day he forked it, and a fork shows interest, not skill).

His own:

- **MandelbrotSwifty**, https://github.com/palimondo/MandelbrotSwifty (Swift, 44 commits, last update 2018-06-03; tags `swift-3.1` of May 2017 and `troubling-sequence` of June 2018). It tries many equivalent ways to write the Mandelbrot set and measures how Swift's compiler treats each: point-free functions over generators in Swift 1, an `Iterator` version in Swift 3, a fluent version with `prefix(while:)`, and hybrids, the goal being functional code as fast as the imperative. Its to-do list ends with moving representative styles into the Swift benchmark suite, and the June 2018 tag matches his forum topics "Troubling `Sequence`" and "Swift's unpredictable efficiency" (section 3). This is a direct, hands-on study of the question Fortress's generators and big operators raise: what lazy, composed functional iteration costs against a loop.
- **BookMinder**, https://github.com/palimondo/BookMinder (Python 3.13 with `uv`, pytest in a behaviour-driven style, `ruff`, `mypy`, pre-commit; 358 commits; last update 2026-09-14): a command-line tool and an MCP connector that give an AI model a reader's Apple Books highlights; its description says it was pair-programmed with Claude Code with test-first development. It is the one recent piece of code of his I saw, and it shows current Python tooling and working with a coding agent.
- **xs**, "Claude Code transcript exploration tools" (Python, 2026-03-05); **video-transcript-lab** (2026-01-24) and **F1-Score** (2026-01-26), with no description on the page; **palimondo.github.io** (Python, 2019-05-16). I did not open them.

His forks, newest first, with the page's descriptions: `fortress` (of `sirinath/fortress`, 2026-10-16, this project's own), `modular` (Mojo and MAX, 2026-09-25), `co-dfns` (a parallel APL compiler, 2026-09-15), `clawdbot` (a personal AI assistant, 2026-01-27), `talk-transcripts` (Clojure talks, 2026-01-24), `quick-data-mcp` (2025-06-01), `buildware-ai` (2024-07-25), `xproc-3.0-specification` (2023-03-28), `swift` (2020-03-04), Lemire's `SwiftWyhash`, `testingRNG` and `SwiftBitset` (random number and bitset code, 2018 and 2019), `swift-evolution` (2019-04-25) and `swift-internals` (2018-04-15). The Swift and Lemire forks are the 2018 to 2020 period; the rest are 2023 to 2026, pointing at AI tooling, array languages (APL) and Mojo, and say where he has looked lately, not what he has built.

## 5. What this says for explaining things to him now

**Where he has hands-on depth** (from the work itself, with dates):

- **Swift as a language and a library**, 2014 to 2020: protocols, generics, the `Sequence` and `Collection` family and why it is hard to get right, `Optional`, strings, value and reference types, the random number API. The Fortress library's traits, generators and reductions are the nearest cousin; an explanation can start from a Swift protocol and say where Fortress differs (dispatch on every argument at run time, juxtaposition as an operator, loops parallel by default).
- **Measuring performance with statistics**, 2017 to 2020: quantiles and the five-number summary, the interquartile-range outlier fence, run-time distributions with several modes, why the minimum can mislead, setup overhead, how many independent runs to trust, the choice between mean and median, noise from the machine against the program's own. He has argued for a nonparametric test (Mann-Whitney) in public. This is the vocabulary to use for microGPT's timings; it needs no definition.
- **Python scripting and tests**, 2017 to 2020 (Python 2.7 and 3 then) and, in 2026, the current toolchain; lit-style test harnesses (which the harness here resembles); build tooling such as GYB.
- **How functional-style code performs under a compiler's optimizer**, from MandelbrotSwifty and the "unpredictable efficiency" thread (2018). A remark on what the Fortress compiler does to a comprehension or a `SUM` lands on experience he has.
- **iOS and Objective-C frameworks**, 2009 to 2014, and the habit of asking how a framework is built inside. Useful for analogies (UIKit's animation blocks), not for this project.

**Where I found no public evidence of depth** (this is absence of evidence in public work; the index of his messages in this project, built beside this note, is the better source on what he knows now):

- **The JVM**: bytecode, class loading, HotSpot, boxing and specialization of generics. Only one Java question, from 2009.
- **Scala**: three learner questions in 2009 to 2010 (the Lift framework, a sequence argument, the cost of a nested method). The checker in this project is Scala; treat him as a reader of it, not a writer.
- **Type-system research**: variance, bounded quantification, a checker's overload rules, multiple dispatch. His pull requests do not touch the Swift compiler's type checker or its optimizer; he worked on the library and the benchmarks around them.
- **Parallel and concurrent programming**: nothing in the public work builds it. His forks of Mojo and a parallel APL compiler (2026) show attention, not practice. Swift before 2020 also had no structured concurrency, so his Swift work predates it.
- **Fortress itself, Rats!, Ant, LaTeX**: no trace.

**How old it is.** Stack Overflow is mostly 2011 to 2014; the benchmark work and the forum are 2017 to mid-2019 (a pull-request sweep ends in April 2020, the closing of unmerged ones in October 2020, one forum post in 2023). That is Swift 1 to 5, before its concurrency and macros. The only recent public code is from 2026 (BookMinder and the transcript tools). So his statistics and benchmark-method knowledge is the sturdiest and the one to rely on; his Swift knowledge is deep but six or more years old; the rest is not shown by this source.

14:## History he knows (do not re-explain)
15-
16-- P-16 **He reads the project's end as the price of doing no work on performance.** DARPA's HPCS did not take Sun into its third phase in 2006, and the project went on at Sun Labs until 2012. The team worked on syntax, and the compiler that was to make the mathematical types fast never came; the funding was cut for good reason.
17-- P-17 **Unboxed doubles and arrays of doubles are required: without them the revival misses its point.** The code generator boxes every number, and boxing is the main cost on microGPT's array kernels (F-11). Boxing is measured on microGPT-shaped kernels, not on a scalar loop with literals and a `:=` accumulator, which microGPT never runs. The storage is P-84's decision; unboxed arithmetic is PLAN phase 6 (P-33).
18-- P-18 **He is coming round to Hsu's view that language paradigms are accidental complexity.**
19-- P-19 **The tree is not described as the third-party port's migration grafted on its history.** The files that still say so wait for the lineage cleanup (PLAN, "Off the path, parked"), which `coordinator/lineage.md`, "Files that still repeat it", lists. His plan to make the graft-free `clean-ladder` branch `main` is not carried out (F-165).
20-
21-## Decisions on record
22-
23-### The standard and the sources
24-
25-- P-25 **The specification stays the standard, the Types chapter beside it.** Where the Types chapter of the team's unfinished 2012 restart (F-166) covers a topic, it is cited beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word. On the rules that the revival revises, it is their latest intent, which the goal is to finish. It covers the exclusion rule, as instantiation exclusion in its two-part form, the `covariant` modifier, and `Bottom`, which no program can write.
26-- P-26 **The type group's late positions outweigh the specification's early text where they conflict.** The early text was a wish. The type group then made the language run, for performance and with specialization a must, and learned what is feasible. So their later word wins: the exclusion rule, specialization kept, the compiler prelude's tower flattened in 2009 and 2010 (P-43), Naden's 2012 write-up, the POPL 2019 paper. The implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text. The revival does not second-guess them: it knows less than they did.
27-- P-27 **The library's own practice is the standard.** What microGPT invented goes into the standard library, in the library's own style. Whoever extends the library first studies how it does the same kind of thing, and follows that pattern; exclusion, for one, is all over it. He had to find the diagonal's override himself (P-88) because that study was skipped. No fix is designed from the specification alone or from a workaround on the user's side.
28-- P-28 **Fleshing out the standard library is a very important task.** Next is the algebraic layer: `Ring`, `Field` and what the matrices and tensors of machine learning need, so that the library's traits reach them. It goes into the standard library itself (P-27), not into a tree of the revival's own.
29-- P-29 **Walk's speed is irrelevant to every judgement of Fortress's performance.** Walk is hundreds of times slower than Python's interpreter. So no performance decision of any kind, and no edit of C4, the flat model program, for speed, until microGPT runs compiled. The gate never runs the two microGPT programs, too long-running to be tests: it compiles them and records the phase that each reaches. A run of them, once possible, goes to a stage that does not gate.
30-- P-30 **The microGPT walk check after a batch runs in under a minute.** It runs about two forward-and-backward passes against the reference values, which shows that the model's mathematics still works and that the library's changes did not break it. The full check programs run only when asked. A slower check is to him a waste of time.
31-- P-32 **The territory map (`coordinator/map/`) maps the tree down to where the design intent is written, in the papers as well as the specification.** It exists so that nothing on record is found again from scratch.
32-- P-33 **The plan (`coordinator/PLAN.md`) has six phases, approved with their workers.** Phases 1 and 2 are landed: the wrapping operators, the revised specification, the run-time sizes, the flat number tower and the overflow natives. 3 is the checker at a true zero; 4, the switch-over, natives then names; 5, microGPT compiles: its static types, the array design and the code generator's holes; 6, microGPT fast. Where the work stands: PLAN's "Where we stand". Re-approval row 41 (ledger row 320: a component named apart from its api does not link) joins the switch-over's design.
33-
34-### The one library and the compiled checker
35-
36-- P-37 **One library, the interpreter's, is the library the compiler checks.** The interpreter's `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin` become the compiled path's library. He sees the compiler's prelude (`CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin`, `CompilerAlgebra`) as a bootstrap to remove, so no declaration goes into it, and its three files are deleted at the switch-over with their tests kept. Code-generator rungs go on. How the checker comes to accept the library is a plan shown to him step by step, not a question to ask again. Still to build: PLAN phase 4.
37-- P-38 **The compiler prelude's defects are not repaired: they go with it at the switch-over.** Its `Maybe` block and its `REM` guard `if other = -1 then 0` stay as landed until the prelude is deleted, and their tests stay. Then the compiled tests respell its reversed wrapping and saturating operators (row 348), `ZZ64`'s compiled shift closes (row 381), and the specification's `shift` reaches the compiled path (row 383). `XXXShiftDeclRungI` is then promoted, and the switch-over batch finds the compiler tests that bind `shift`, a reserved name from then on. Still to build: PLAN phase 4.
38-- P-39 **The checker count is measured in every gate and never turns the gate red.** The gate reports the count stage on its own. The distance to the switch-over (F-53), over all apis and components, is a report-only stage of the phase-3 gates, whose work drives it down.
39-- P-40 **Sizes are checked, and a size left unknown is an error only where it is used.** The checker checks `nat` and `int` static parameters and refuses a size beyond `NN32` or `ZZ32` (F-140). Storage refuses a JVM array length over 2^31-1. A size that inference leaves unknown is an error only when it reaches a type, a name or a value. How the checker represents it is not his choice. A size that a call cannot fix refuses the call, also inside an overload set, instead of dropping the arm (row 400, its compiled half open). Every static argument but an operator counts in the exclusion rule; booleans join once the checker has boolean parameters (row 406). A size used as a value converts to `ZZ32` as a numeral does (row 485). The api's 25 unused sizes (F-35) go only by a diff shown to him with the switch-over's design.
40-- P-41 **At run time a size travels as the descriptor that a type argument has (design B).** It fills the slot that the team's code generator reserved. Each number has one descriptor, from a table, with no holder class, as the team instantiates types. Operator static arguments stay compile-time names (F-39): he sees no need to unify them.
41-- P-42 **An unbounded type parameter's implicit bound is `Any`, not `Object`.** `Any` holds tuples, functions and `()`, which `Object` does not, and the library instantiates its generic containers at tuples, arrays indexed by pairs among them. The specification states the bound, with a callout that keeps the Working Draft's `Object`. The compile path's `Object` bound departs from it until the switch-over (row 412).
42-- P-43 **The exclusion rule stays, and the number tower is flat (route A).** The compiled checker keeps the multiple instantiation exclusion rule. So the library's numbers are flat, as the team (Chase, Ryu, Maessen and Allen) flattened the compiler prelude in 2009 and 2010. The fixed widths, `ZZ`, `QQ` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`, each with its own algebra, and `Number` has no catch-all operators. Why: the flattened prelude is the team's last record of the Fortress way, and its route leads to the POPL 2019 paper, which keeps the rule. He cares that specialised code runs fast, not how a specialisation is chosen. F-46 prices a return to route C.
43-- P-44 **`AnyIntegral`'s closure stands, and the checker reads `comprises` the 2012 way.** The closure `AnyIntegral comprises { ... }` stands, with a `NOT YET` comment in the team's wording. So do the generic scalar-extension block, the `AnyAdditiveGroup` marker and the `Array3` exclusion. A generic child of a closed trait may extend it when every type that the checker knows below it is listed. The clause's text and walk stay as they are. Row 487 records the hole that every reading but the 2008 one shares: a program's own `Integral` subtype in another component is not caught.
44-- P-45 **Overloads may differ in their static parameters (answer 9).** The specification drops its sentence that forbids it and states the type group's 2011 model, which the checker runs; the old sentence stays as superseded text. The checker keeps the paper's three overloading rules, checks the Return Type Rule over every instance, and requires two generic declarations in the more-specific relation to agree on their static parameters position by position, as Java's overriding rule does (row 398). Walk dispatches on declared domains, not by the order of the declarations. The library repairs its refused families with its own exclusions, and no model line changes. The judgement's smaller choices took the record's defaults, listed for his review in `PLAN.md`.
45-- P-46 **A conversion makes a call possible, and never changes which declaration runs when one already fits.** Declarations are chosen on declared domains, by applicability and then specificity (P-45). The chosen one is instantiated by answer 8's promotion (P-74), its coercions inserted statically. So beside a plain arm over `Any`, a generic arm over `T extends Number` runs at `ZZ64` for a mixed-width call. A numeral whose candidate types are incomparable reads as `ZZ32`, or as `ZZ64` or `ZZ` by its magnitude. Why: generic code is never fast, and he wants code that a JVM can specialise. His own broader rule, to convert toward a specific declaration before a generic one, is not taken. Both paths infer static arguments with coercion and the same promotion, and P-49 orders the checker's attempts. Still open: the dispatch between two generic declarations (row 537, PLAN phase 5).
46-- P-47 **Each integer type declares its own `MIN`, `MAX` and `MINMAX`.** It follows `QQ`, `RR64`, the compiler library and the specification's `ZZ`, so that under walk the family answers at the promoted type. Row 484's `NN32` half, a numeral beside an `NN32`, is still open.
47-- P-48 **A type parameter that a call's arguments do not fix takes its bound, never `Bottom`.** Its instance is the intersection of its upper bounds, constrained by the call's static return type, never the arguments' union or the value's type alone. The rule is the team's later word (POPL 2019). He ranks the team's later work above his own reading. It sets the instance, not which declaration runs (P-46). MicroGPT's types are concrete, so it is untouched. The library keeps the team's unbounded declarations. Built under walk for a reduction or comprehension that writes no static argument by climb batch 15 (`20474c144`). Still to build: a compiled dispatcher that carries the static return type (row 538, PLAN phase 5).
48-- P-49 **The checker tries a call without the expected type first, and with coercion only after (row 508).** It keeps the first attempt, by subtyping, when its result converts to the expected type, and only then tries coercion with the context. So a declaration that fits the arguments as they are is not passed over for one reached by coercion.

So the checker passes the expected type of the whole into the body and into the exits' values, as for a `typecase` clause, and the inference chapter lists both contexts. P-51 is the other half of item 48. Row 642 stays `CONTESTED` only because the ledger's tool cannot close it.

Its probe moves no error of the distance. Its rung promotes the expected failures `XXXInferContextDrops` and `XXXInferLoneUnionClosedTrait`, whose refusals it repairs. # The form for putting an open design question to Pavol

## 1. The shape of the message

Every instance that worked is one chat message (never a rendered page, never a link
for a single decision — a rendered page is used only for a whole plan or document, e.g.
the coordinator's page for `PLAN.md`, POSITIONS 2026-09-26) with five parts, always in
this order:

1. **The question**, named and restated in one line ("Batch-5 answer 2: do sizes and
   boolean arguments count in the exclusion rule?").
2. **Context**, as short bullets: what the rule/spec says, what each path does today,
   what the library already does in the family, what the ledger row records. This is
   protocol.md principle 2's evidence order (`protocol.md:61-74`: mathematics, each path
   measured, the specification, the library's own practice and where the designers
   departed from Java, the peers, the commits, then the derivation).
3. **The options**, numbered, each one line: what it is and what it costs or forecloses.
4. **The ask**, naming one option by number, with "Yes: ... No: ..." spelling out
   exactly what a yes commits him to and what a no does instead.
5. **The recommendation**, one line, last, never in place of the explanation
   ("I recommend option 1: ...").

This is written down in two places, neither of which names all five parts together:
- `protocol.md:76-79` (principle 3): "One ask per message: what the work would do, what
  it touches, what it costs, what a yes commits him to; the recommendation last and
  never instead of the explanation."
- `POSITIONS.md:133` ("Asks and decisions"): "An ask for a yes states, in the message
  itself, what the worker would do, what it produces, what it touches in the tree, what
  it costs, what the yes commits him to afterwards and what a no costs; one ask per
  message; no label stands in for an explanation ... the recommendation comes after the
  explanation, in one line, never instead of it."

Length in the working instances runs about 1,500 to 3,300 characters (batch-5 answers
1-3: 1,889 / 2,445 / 2,209 chars). When a question needs a refresher because it touches
something he does not already know (a design's purpose, how peers do it), the message
grows to 4,700-5,000 chars but keeps the same five-part order with the refresher
inserted between context and options (answer 6's second try, 4,766 chars; the row-40
re-explanation, 4,990 chars).

## 2. Five instances, timestamps and exact words

**Batch-5 answer 1 (worked, first try).** Ask at 2026-09-26T09:08:39Z, opening line "Four
Opus workers have been running since 09:08 UTC: ... While they run, here is the first of
the five batch-5 answers. **What should rung S's citations call the unrevised copy?**"
Ends "**The ask:** option 1. ... I recommend option 1: it's the team's own form, and the
name is accurate." Reply at 2026-09-26T09:19:58Z (11 min later): "Option 1, agreed."

**Row 40 (failed, then fixed by naming the form).** First, terse try at

note left three questions ... What I propose: close row 40 as 'not a decision taken' ...

  he could take or refuse in one reply; this is the instance he flagged as the form not
  being used.

## 4. Whether the form is written down

Yes, in general terms, in two places, but not as one named checklist:
- `protocol.md:76-79` (principle 3): one ask per message, what the work would do, what
  it touches, what it costs, what a yes commits to, recommendation last.
- `protocol.md:61-74` (principle 2): the evidence order a design question is answered
  from before it reaches him — mathematics, each path measured, the specification, the
  library's own practice, the peers, the commits, then the derivation and the decision.
- `POSITIONS.md:133` ("Asks and decisions"): the same rule in his own words, with the

What is not written down anywhere: the numbered-options-with-an-explicit-"yes/no"-ask
layout itself (as distinct from the general "what it does/costs/commits" principle), and
the rule that when the context assumes knowledge he lacks, a refresher and a peer survey
go in before the options (this was reconstructed here from the row-40 and answer-6
instances; `restate-and-hold.md` and `wall-of-text-spiral.md` cover the adjacent but
different failure of length/register during rapid back-and-forth reading, not this one).

# The wall of text spiral: instances and recoveries

The pattern: Pavol reads the coordinator's turns one at a time from mobile and
replies to each; the coordinator answers every remark at length; the replies
pile up faster than he can read them; he has to stop and issue a recovery
command. He has named it this exact phrase at least four times: 2026-08-21,
2026-08-30, 2026-09-19, 2026-09-21.

## The instances

feedback, shot acknowledgment of reception. I need to recover from the wall of

after: 235 characters, then short turns (151, 223, 32, 110). Same evening, at

scrolling back up to continue reading the wall of text"*; *"I think we're in an

**2026-09-19, 14:51:07Z** (`transcripts-blinded:fe616d40...`). Two lists precede

characters, a review's findings, argued in prose). After reading the second for
over an hour: *"And this is a wall of text that I cannot absorb at this
moment... I have a executive function depletion."* Reply after: 1,494
characters, still prose; he pushes back again at 14:53:20 (*"smart alloc
register"*); the next reply, "Plain version. Six decisions." (14:53:40), is a

## What recovered each one

Each time, the same shape worked: stop writing argument and prose, hand back a
list of items short enough to be "what we do, what it changes, a default" — not

being read at all (*"go"* to a default, not to a document). 09-20 recovered

says 'hold', acknowledge in three lines, add his point to this list, and reply
nothing else until he says he has finished reading."* Kept current through five
further boots (through `2bae1d391`, 09-23); nothing in it has been folded into

## Rules already on record, and whether they held

- `protocol.md` §3 (from the 08-21 reconstruction): *"Feedback arrives in
  batches, often from mobile. Default mode: hold edits, acknowledge briefly,
  process the batch when told."* On record since the first instance — still
  violated on 2026-09-20, five times in one hour. Stating it once did not

- The sharper version — three lines, add to the held list, nothing else until
  told to stop — exists only in `held-list.md`'s boot note (09-20), never
  merged into `protocol.md`. It held better afterward: the 09-21 self-catch was
  one flagged turn, not a chain, and no further spiral appears through 09-23.
- POSITIONS.md, 2026-09-20 (line 63): brief replies, plain English, no jargon,
  no register, decisions one at a time with a default he can accept without
  reading the argument.
- POSITIONS.md, 2026-09-22 (lines 70–71): *"table formatted in this way is hard
  to read on mobile... we just need a list"*; and re-approval rows taken *"one
  per message with refreshers... not in groups."* Applied through 09-23 with no
  recorded spiral since — the rule that has held best.
- The held list itself needs one more guard, from 01:14:56: an item on it is
  not thereby settled or safe to drop silently; it still needs an answer.

## A rule for the protocol, in plain words

While Pavol is reading and replying turn by turn, the coordinator answers each
remark in a few short lines — no argument, no new analysis, no register — and
writes more only when he asks a direct question that needs it. The moment he
says "hold" or anything like it, every open point goes onto one list in the
order raised, and nothing else is written until he says he is done reading;
each listed item still gets answered when he asks for it, not filed and
forgotten. Decisions reach him one at a time, as what we'd do and what it
changes, with a default he can take without reading the reasoning, which stays
in a committed document, not the chat reply. Lists, never tables. A reply
running long while he is mid-read is itself the signal to stop and ask
whether he wants the list instead of the rest of the prose.

# Q1 of climb batch 16: the detour toward Scala's way

## In short

- **The question.** May the compiled checker refuse `object O extends { A, B }`, where `A` declares `pick(self)` abstract and `B` gives it a body, and `O` declares none of its own (rows 572 and 727)?
- **The answer.** Refuse it (P-149), the curator's word of 06:23 UTC: the specification's text and the type group's later calculus refuse it, and the revival does not bend Fortress toward another language for a convenience.
- **The detour.** The ask put to the curator led him toward Scala's way, which accepts `O`. He pre-recorded it, then learnt that the specification refuses `O`, and took the refusal.
- **Its cost.** About 1.7M tokens written: the probe 0.56M, and this session 1.17M, nearly all of it two rewrites of its 550K context into the cache after the VM restart and after a gap of nearly two hours.
- **The causes.** The ask did not say first what the designers' text says and which way it points. It named a peer language's behaviour as if it were an option of equal standing. It used the record's shorthand. And the fact that would decide the question, whether the library uses the shape, was not measured before the ask.

## The question

A functional method has `self` among its parameters and is called like a function, `pick(x)`. A trait may leave one abstract, with no body:

```
trait A  pick(self): String  end           (* abstract *)
trait B  pick(self): String = "b"  end     (* a body *)
object O extends { A, B } end              (* no pick of its own *)
```

Today the compiled path accepts `O` and runs `B`'s body, because its overloading check skips a component's own abstract functional methods (`OverloadingChecker.scala:139-141`). Walk refuses `O` at load (F-142). Separately, an abstract and a concrete declaration of one method in one trait pass the checker and crash the code generator (row 727).

## How it went, in UTC

- **01:08 to 01:37.** Batch 16's planner drafted Q1 with the default "refuse" (rung K builds it), and listed the sources: the specification, the type group's rules, the team's dotted-method check and Java refuse; the team's abstract-method check and Scala accept. Its brief told it to run no new probe, so the record left the library's use of the shape to rung K's own run.
- **01:38 to 02:11.** The Fable review agreed that Q1 is the curator's.
- **02:13.** The coordinator put Q1 to the curator. The ask used the record's words ("batch 8's judge", "item 62", "read them", "leave them unread"), gave the sources as a split without saying that the specification's text refuses `O`, and gave as the refusal's cost that it "gives up Scala's way of letting a sibling trait supply the body".
- **04:18.** The curator found the ask unreadable past its primer, leaned to Scala's way if it had a clean resolution, and asked why the library's use of the shape had not been measured, "the most important factor for the decision".
- **04:19.** The coordinator launched the probe (`perf-probes/abstract-sibling-body/`).
- **06:10 to 06:13.** While it ran, the curator pre-recorded Scala's way, unless hard evidence against it surfaced (P-149, first form).
- **06:14.** The curator, who had listened to the ask in a car, asked whether the specification declared this way. The coordinator told him that it refuses `O`, and held P-149.
- **06:17.** The probe reported. The curator asked why the work had gone toward Scala's way at all, if the specification and the implementations agreed. They did not agree: the compiled path accepts `O`, walk refuses it, and one of the team's own checks (`AbstractMethodChecker.scala:94-107`) counts an inherited body as the implementation. Scala had entered only as the coordinator's comparison.
- **06:23.** The curator took the refusal.

## What the probe found

From `explorations/perf-probes/abstract-sibling-body/REPORT.md`:

- **Neither library uses the shape.** No type in the one library or the compiler's library inherits an abstract functional method and a sibling's body without providing their meet. With the checker's filter lifted, the count and distance stages are unchanged.
- **Scala's way is buildable for equal types.** It takes one exemption in the checker and two edits in walk, and nothing in the code generator. It needs two passages of the specification rewritten. A narrower return type or an api boundary reaches code-generator defects (rows 732 to 735).
- **The designers' word refuses `O`.** The specification's text refuses it. The type group's Welterweight calculus (2012) refuses it too, the work behind P-147. POPL 2019 has no abstract methods. Java refuses `O`; Scala accepts it.
- **The record had stale claims.** Walk refuses `O` at load and no longer stops at a call. The compiler's library declares abstract functional methods in its api (`CompilerBuiltin.fsi:37-40`). Welterweight admits an abstract and a concrete declaration at one domain, so "every source refuses row 727" is overstated.

## What changes

- **P-149** records the refusal and the curator's rule behind it: other languages are consulted only to reconcile a conflict between the designers' earlier and later choices.
- **Climb batch 16's rung K** stays as drafted. Before the splice, its record takes the probe's corrections: walk's refusal at load, the compiler's library's abstract api declarations, and the wording on row 727.
- **The ledger** has the probe's four rows, 732 to 735.
- **For the `coordinator` skill** (held for the skill writer):
  - An ask states first what the designers' text and their later word say, and which way they point. A peer language's behaviour enters only where the designers' earlier and later choices conflict.
  - The coordinator runs the probe that a planner names for a question before putting the question to the curator.
  - The ask's plain words are already a rule. Here it was not followed.
- **This session's cost of a cold turn.** With its context near 580K, a turn after an hour's gap or a restart rewrites about 0.55M into the cache. A compaction before a long gap cuts that.

import json, re, sys
msgs = json.load(open('msgs.json'))
ev = open('/home/user/fortress/explorations/coordinator/curator-profile/evidence.md').read().split('\n')
area = None; areas = {}
for l in ev:
    m = re.match(r'## (\d)\. ', l)
    if m: area = int(m.group(1)); continue
    if l.startswith('## '): area = None
    m = re.match(r'- (\d{4}-\d\d-\d\dT\d\d:\d\d:\d\d)Z · ([^·]+) · (.*)', l)
    if m and area:
        areas.setdefault(area, []).append((m.group(1), m.group(2).strip(), m.group(3)))
for a, ents in areas.items():
    out = open('area%d.txt' % a, 'w')
    done = set()
    tot = 0
    for ts, kind, label in ents:
        hits = [m for m in msgs if m['ts'].startswith(ts)]
        out.write('##### %s [%s] %s\n' % (ts, kind, label))
        if ts in done:
            out.write('(printed above)\n\n'); continue
        done.add(ts)
        for m in hits:
            out.write(m['text'].strip() + '\n')
            tot += len(m['text'])
        out.write('\n')
    out.close()
    print(a, len(ents), tot)
EOF

cd /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-fortress/fe616d40-a9c6-56d7-9da1-7168a172765d/scratchpad && cat > byarea.py <<'EOF'
import json, re, sys
msgs = json.load(open('msgs.json'))
ev = open('/home/user/fortress/explorations/coordinator/curator-profile/evidence.md').read().split('\n')
area = None; areas = {}
for l in ev:
    m = re.match(r'## (\d)\. ', l)
    if m: area = int(m.group(1)); continue
    if l.startswith('## '): area = None
    m = re.match(r'- (\d{4}-\d\d-\d\dT\d\d:\d\d:\d\d)Z · ([^·]+) · (.*)', l)
    if m and area:
        areas.setdefault(area, []).append((m.group(1), m.group(2).strip(), m.group(3)))
for a, ents in areas.items():
    out = open('area%d.txt' % a, 'w')
    done = set()
    tot = 0
    for ts, kind, label in ents:
        hits = [m for m in msgs if m['ts'].startswith(ts)]
        out.write('##### %s [%s] %s\n' % (ts, kind, label))
        if ts in done:
            out.write('(printed above)\n\n'); continue
        done.add(ts)
        for m in hits:
            out.write(m['text'].strip() + '\n')
            tot += len(m['text'])
        out.write('\n')
    out.close()
    print(a, len(ents), tot)
EOF
python3 -I byarea.py; wc -c area*.txt

27:- P-27 **The library's own practice is the standard.** What microGPT invented goes into the standard library, in the library's own style. Whoever extends the library first studies how it does the same kind of thing, and follows that pattern; exclusion, for one, is all over it. He had to find the diagonal's override himself (P-88) because that study was skipped. No fix is designed from the specification alone or from a workaround on the user's side.
64:- P-149 **An object that inherits an abstract functional method from one trait and its body from a sibling trait, and declares none of its own, is refused (Q1).** So `object O extends { A, B }`, with `pick(self)` abstract in `A` and given a body in `B`, must declare its own `pick`, as the specification's text and the type group's Welterweight calculus require and as walk already does; an abstract and a concrete declaration of one method in one trait are refused too. Why: the revival honors the designers' intent and does not change Fortress's nature for a convenience; other languages are consulted only to reconcile a conflict between earlier and later designers' choices, and here there is none. No library type uses the shape. Still to build: climb batch 16's rung K, rows 572 and 727.
89:- P-87 **The model's text is the notation, and the vocabulary is repaired around it.** An operator in the model never becomes a function call to satisfy an overload check. Any repair that changes a model line is shown to him as a diff before it is built. Decision D, the sized signatures of the flat program C4's vocabulary, is such a diff (`reviews/decision-d-diff.md`); nothing of it is applied before PLAN phase 5.
90:- P-88 **The model's vocabulary leaves `+`, `-` and `MAX` between an array and a scalar to the library's scalar block, and its diagonal keeps its own product.** `Diag` extends `Matrix` and overrides `mul`, as the type system promises (row 299). A read-only matrix trait, `ReadableArray2` under `Array2`, is a library change for a later ledger row, not a vocabulary hack.
168:- F-165 **The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, and `main` descends from `8fe1daa8f`, which copied a third-party Java 9 port onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`.** The port shares no history with this tree, and most of its 1,506 files are removed or redone. One running piece stays, the `FTypeArrayList` fix for the JDK 8 `TreeSet` crash; `lineage.md` lists the rest for removal. The branch `clean-ladder` (`8332bd34f`) rebuilds on `a874948ac` without the port and never replaced `main`. Detail: `coordinator/lineage.md`, "The facts".

# What Pavol knows: a profile for the coordinator

Built on 2026-10-16 from `evidence.md` (an index of 997 entries into his 1,946 messages) and `public-work.md`, both beside this file, with the messages behind the entries read in full. Section 4 is the checklist to use before an explanation or an ask. The sections before it are its ground.

- "Knows" means that a message shows the knowledge. It doesn't mean that the knowledge is deep.
- `POSITIONS.md`, "History he knows (do not re-explain)", holds what he knows of the project's history. This file doesn't repeat it.

## 1. Who he is, in short

1. He's a software engineer, not a language researcher. He has a master's degree from the Technical University of Košice (2004). He works in Central European time, often late into the night.
2. He calls the revival his hobby: a spare-time exercise in learning Fortress and agentic coding. It started as a test of the claim that coding is solved. He says that the intelligence in the work comes from the model, and that he directs it without deep expertise. He took on microGPT partly to learn how language models and their mathematics work.
3. He came to Fortress through Steele's 2016 talks, and "Four Solutions" is the one he remembers most. His first plan was to extend Fortress with complex numbers, after an earlier chat ported his Mandelbrot toy program to Fortress. He calls that program Scala once and Swift once; his public `MandelbrotSwifty` is Swift. He dropped the plan when the compiler proved unfinished.
4. In his own words: he used Scala 2.8 at a startup and loves it, and he worked extensively on Swift's benchmark suite.
5. Stack Overflow (`palimondo`, 2008 to 2023): 45 answers, 34 of them from 2011 to 2014, mostly on iOS and Objective-C. Scala shows as three learner's questions and one answer, from 2009 and 2010. That answer is his highest-voted one. Two of the questions ask what a Scala feature costs.
6. Swift, 2017 to 2020: about 88 merged pull requests to the benchmark suite. They hold Python tooling with unit tests (`BenchmarkDriver`, `BenchmarkDoctor`), the Swift driver's sampling, and the statistics of measurement: quantiles, the interquartile outlier fence, run times with several modes, how many independent samples make a change believable. He also sped up a random-number function of the standard library. None of his pull requests touches the compiler's C++, its type checker or its optimizer. On the Swift forums (2017 to 2019) he wrote about benchmarks, then about the design of `Sequence`, `Collection` and the random-number API.
7. `MandelbrotSwifty` (2017 to 2018) measures what composed, generator-style iteration costs against a plain loop. That is the question that Fortress's generators and big operators raise. His only recent public code (2026) is Python, written with Claude Code.
8. Relayed and not verified: a Claude chat's memory summary that he pasted adds over 20 years in software, current work as a product owner and technical contractor, an iPhone weather app (2015) and a port of a hash function to Swift.
9. He writes English by dictation. He speaks Slovak around him, and once a German phrase slips in.

### 2.2 Type systems and language design

**Knows, as practical judgement.**

1. Coercion: an implicit conversion between operand types, tried only when no declaration fits by subtyping. Flat number siblings need pairwise conversions, and a narrower number that fits a wider one converts directly. He asked to have his vocabulary corrected, then used it correctly.
2. `Any` is the type of every value, and `Object` leaves out `()`, which he first had to ask about.
3. Java erases generic types; Fortress keeps them, so its class loader chooses at run time.
4. Dispatch on the types of all operands is Fortress's defining feature, and exclusion declarations are all over the library.
5. A type that declares conformance to the library's traits gets behavior for free. His anchor is the complex-number Mandelbrot. He judges a design by its ergonomics and code reuse for users, not by type-theoretic purity.
6. He proposes designs by analogy: the diagonal as a subtype of matrix with its own product (it became P-88), and a read-only matrix trait.
7. A `where` clause narrows where a declaration applies. He asks whether building it risks soundness, and he knows of the 2016 unsoundness of Java and Scala through `null`.
8. He applies the rule that the team's later word outweighs their earlier text, over his own reading (P-26, P-48).

## 4. Before an explanation or an ask

**Take as known.**

3. Fortress's big ideas: dispatch on all arguments, juxtaposition, parallel by default, traits that give behavior, flat number siblings with coercion, `Any` against `Object`, boxing as the cost, walk against the compiled path, caches keyed by path.

**Explain from the ground up, each time.**

4. Any question of the type system. Start from a concrete Fortress program and several cases of it. Say first what the specification and the team's later word say, and which way they point. Then give the library's practice, and then what the peers do, as context only, never as an option of equal standing (P-149). Say what each option does for a compiled, fast microGPT (P-8). 6. The number types, if they come up again: from the bottom up, `ZZ32` first.
7. The run-time class loader and its descriptors. Start from his own picture: Swift's mangled names, and the loader stamping sizes into a class so that the JIT can drop bounds checks.
8. The checker count and the distance to the switch-over: what each counts, and why one can jump.
9. Each Fortress construct that he hasn't met: `label` and `exit`, `where`, `comprises`, `atomic`, `()`, nat parameters and `reflect`.

13. Loose time words ("yesterday", "this morning"), "we" for him and Claude, "the" at the start of a glossary entry, and a closing coda.

14. Brevity against detail: he demands short replies, yet he praised a long, detailed reply when facts were being established. The evidence fits a length set by the mode, not a fixed one.
15. He says he hasn't read the specification, the papers or the library, yet he has spot-checked the specification and the array code, and he recalls Steele's talks precisely. What he has read is nowhere listed.
16. He says he knows no type theory, yet he reasons soundly about coercion, bounds and erasure. The evidence shows practical judgement, not formal training.
17. He says Scala earned him most of his Stack Overflow points. The public record shows that his highest-voted answer is a Scala one, but that most of the account is iOS and Objective-C.

19. He wants to own every choice, and at times he takes a default unread ("I have no idea what I'm deciding on, but let's push forward to zero").

Built on 2026-10-16 from `evidence.md` (an index of 997 entries into his 1,946 messages) and `public-work.md`, both beside this file, with the messages behind the entries read in full. Section 4 is the checklist to use before an explanation or an ask. The sections before it are its ground.

## 1. Who he is, in short

1. He's a software engineer, not a language researcher. He has a master's degree from the Technical University of Košice (2004). He works in Central European time, often late into the night.
2. He calls the revival his hobby: a spare-time exercise in learning Fortress and agentic coding. It started as a test of the claim that coding is solved. He says that the intelligence in the work comes from the model, and that he directs it without deep expertise. He took on microGPT partly to learn how language models and their mathematics work.
3. He came to Fortress through Steele's 2016 talks, and "Four Solutions" is the one he remembers most. His first plan was to extend Fortress with complex numbers, after an earlier chat ported his Mandelbrot toy program to Fortress. He calls that program Scala once and Swift once; his public `MandelbrotSwifty` is Swift. He dropped the plan when the compiler proved unfinished.
4. In his own words: he used Scala 2.8 at a startup and loves it, and he worked extensively on Swift's benchmark suite.
5. Stack Overflow (`palimondo`, 2008 to 2023): 45 answers, 34 of them from 2011 to 2014, mostly on iOS and Objective-C. Scala shows as three learner's questions and one answer, from 2009 and 2010. That answer is his highest-voted one. Two of the questions ask what a Scala feature costs.

He also sped up a random-number function of the standard library. None of his pull requests touches the compiler's C++, its type checker or its optimizer. On the Swift forums (2017 to 2019) he wrote about benchmarks, then about the design of `Sequence`, `Collection` and the random-number API.
7. `MandelbrotSwifty` (2017 to 2018) measures what composed, generator-style iteration costs against a plain loop. That is the question that Fortress's generators and big operators raise. His only recent public code (2026) is Python, written with Claude Code.
8. Relayed and not verified: a Claude chat's memory summary that he pasted adds over 20 years in software, current work as a product owner and technical contractor, an iPhone weather app (2015) and a port of a hash function to Swift.
9. He writes English by dictation. He speaks Slovak around him, and once a German phrase slips in.

### 2.2 Type systems and language design

**Knows, as practical judgement.**

2. `Any` is the type of every value, and `Object` leaves out `()`, which he first had to ask about.
3. Java erases generic types; Fortress keeps them, so its class loader chooses at run time.
4. Dispatch on the types of all operands is Fortress's defining feature, and exclusion declarations are all over the library.
5. A type that declares conformance to the library's traits gets behavior for free. His anchor is the complex-number Mandelbrot. He judges a design by its ergonomics and code reuse for users, not by type-theoretic purity.
6. He proposes designs by analogy: the diagonal as a subtype of matrix with its own product (it became P-88), and a read-only matrix trait.
7. A `where` clause narrows where a declaration applies. He asks whether building it risks soundness, and he knows of the 2016 unsoundness of Java and Scala through `null`.

1	<!-- What Pavol, the curator, knows and where his gaps are, by area and by date, drawn from his messages of 2026-08-18 to 2026-10-16 and his public work, for the coordinating session to read before it explains something to him or puts a question to him. -->
2	
3	# What Pavol knows: a profile for the coordinator
4	
5	Built on 2026-10-16 from `evidence.md` (997 entries into his 1,946 messages) and `public-work.md`, both beside this file, with the indexed messages read in full. Section 4 is the checklist; the rest is its ground.
6	
7	- Times are UTC, in 2026, written month-day hour:minute. `python3 -I explorations/coordinator/curator-profile/show.py 2026-09-15T09:49` prints his messages of that minute.
8	- "Knows" means a message shows it, not that it is deep.
9	- `POSITIONS.md`, "History he knows (do not re-explain)", holds what he knows of the project's history. This file doesn't repeat it.
10	
11	## 1. Who he is, in short
12	
13	1. A software engineer, not a language researcher, with a master's degree from the Technical University of Košice (2004). He works in Central European time, at times late into the night.
14	2. He calls the revival his hobby: spare-time learning about Fortress and agentic coding, begun as a test of the claim that coding is solved. He says the intelligence in the work is the model's and that he directs it without deep expertise. He took on microGPT partly to learn how language models and their mathematics work.
15	3. He came to Fortress through Steele's 2016 talks; "Four Solutions" is the one he remembers most. His first plan, complex numbers in Fortress after a chat ported his Mandelbrot toy program, ended when the compiler proved unfinished. He calls that program Scala once and Swift once.
16	4. In his words: Scala 2.8 at a startup, a language he loves; Swift, where he worked extensively on the benchmark suite.
17	5. Stack Overflow (`palimondo`): 45 answers, mostly 2011 to 2014 and mostly iOS and Objective-C. Scala shows as three learner's questions and one answer (2009, 2010), his highest-voted. From 2010 he asks what a feature costs.
18	6. Swift, 2017 to 2020: about 88 merged pull requests to the benchmark suite. Python tooling with unit tests (`BenchmarkDriver`, `BenchmarkDoctor`), the driver's sampling, and the statistics of measurement: quantiles, the interquartile outlier fence, run times with several modes, how many independent samples make a change believable. None that the search found touches the compiler's C++, type checker or optimizer. On the forums he wrote about benchmarks and the design of `Sequence` and `Collection`.
19	7. `MandelbrotSwifty` (2017, 2018) measures what generator-style iteration costs against a loop, the question that Fortress's generators and big operators raise. His only recent public code (2026) is Python written with Claude Code.
20	8. Relayed, not verified (a Claude chat's memory summary he pasted): over 20 years in software, now a product owner and technical contractor.
21	9. He writes English by dictation, and speaks Slovak around him.

It is about 25.1K characters, a little over the 25K limit. Its first line is a one-sentence header comment. It has the four sections asked for, and each section ends with its list of timestamps. I read every indexed message in full before I wrote anything.

The checklist (section 4), in short:
1. **Take as known:** the History section of POSITIONS and his decisions; Swift's language and library; measurement statistics; Python; git; lit-style tests; the Claude Code client; Fortress's big ideas (dispatch on all arguments, flat numbers with coercion, `Any` against `Object`, boxing as the cost). Cite a decision by what it says, never by its number: he often doesn't recall rulings by label.
2. **Type questions:** start from a concrete Fortress program and several cases. Say first what the specification and the team's later word say. 3. **Matrix algebra, rings and fields, the dot product:** nothing has stuck in a month. Start from a 2×2 matrix times a vector and microGPT's real matrix shapes, which are not square.
4. **Also explain each time:** number types from the bottom up (ZZ32 first); the class loader from his own picture (Swift's mangled names, sizes stamped into a class); the checker count against the distance to the switch-over; constructs he hasn't met (`label`, `where`, `comprises`, `atomic`, `()`). When he's tired, give one item and a default.
5. **Words to avoid:** bare numbers or letters of entries, items, rows, rungs and batches; "judge", "closure", "sealed", "the line"; undefined math terms ("tensor", "ravel"); loose time words; "we" for him and Claude.
6. **Contradictions the evidence leaves unsettled:** he wants short replies but praised a long one when facts were being set; he says he hasn't read the sources yet spot-checks them; he says he knows no type theory yet reasons soundly about it; he wants to own every choice yet at times takes a default unread.
7. **Two facts that disagree with him:** his memory of `main`'s history differs from F-165, and his Scala-versus-iOS account of his Stack Overflow record differs from the public record. His claims about other languages (for example Swift's witness tables) are unchecked.
